strengths: SIL addresses a meaningful robustness problem: learning one invariant feature can leave a model vulnerable when that feature becomes unobservable. The motivating examples and H-CMNIST construction communicate this distinction clearly.

H-CMNIST provides direct evidence of improved learning of an additional feature. After removing color, ASGDRO achieves 69.17% shape-only accuracy versus GDRO’s 61.44%, and 66.62% versus 57.53% when the spurious box remains (Table 1).

The empirical evaluation is broad and demonstrates practical usefulness. Worst-group accuracy improves over GDRO from 90.6% to 91.4% on Waterbirds and from 87.2% to 91.0% on CelebA. DPLCLIP+ASGDRO reaches a 74.0% DomainBed average versus 72.6% for DPLCLIP and 72.9% for DPLCLIP+GDRO (Tables 2 and 4).

The optimizer combines established ASAM and GDRO components in a reusable way. The appendices provide multiple-seed results, substantial hyperparameter details, and a clear distinction between training-domain and oracle model selection.
weaknesses: Theorem 1’s characterization of the minimizers is incorrect as stated. In Appendix A.4, take the stated Z=(1,...,1), θ=λ with sum λ=1, and Y=1. Under the stated Euclidean perturbation constraint, max R(λ+ε)=pρ²/2 for every λ. A singleton predictor and the uniform mixture therefore have identical robust loss. The proof introduces a λ-dependent gradient factor without justification and treats a first-order approximation as equality. This invalidates the central claimed guarantee of balanced feature use.

The connection between feature invariance and parameter flatness has additional substantive gaps. Joint conditional invariance in Definition 1 does not generally imply invariance for every subset, as Section 3.1 asserts. Equation 4 also equates maximization over particular invariant mechanisms with maximization over an entire parameter ball; containment supplies an inequality, not that equality. Furthermore, Proposition 1’s gradient-norm approximation does not establish convergence to flat minima: sharp stationary points also have zero gradient.

The evaluated algorithm differs materially from the analyzed objective. Algorithm 1 and Equation 8 use separate adversarial perturbations for each environment, whereas Section 4.3 states that every non-toy experiment uses one perturbation computed from average empirical risk. Environment gradients can cancel, so this substitution need not expose worst-environment sharpness. No comparison or theoretical justification validates the substitution. Together with the theorem failure, this determines my weak-reject recommendation despite the useful empirical gains.

Evidence for the specific SIL mechanism is narrower than the benchmark coverage suggests. H-CMNIST is the only direct feature-removal experiment, and its shape-only result has substantial variability (69.17±6.19% over three seeds). The real-image experiments evaluate distribution shifts without controlled removal of invariant attributes. Broader Grad-CAM activation and lower Hessian eigenvalues do not establish that multiple independent predictive features are used or that their removal is tolerated.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the useful appendix details. H-CMNIST lacks explicit sample counts, split construction, and a model-selection criterion; Appendix A.8 does not provide comparable training configurations for the additional WILDS experiments. Many baseline results are imported from prior papers, limiting assessment of matched tuning budgets. These are secondary reporting concerns rather than the primary reasons for rejection.
